The Greenland halibut Reinhardtius hippoglossoides exhibits a life history shaped by its deep, cold-water environment in the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans. Hatchlings emerge from demersal eggs at a small size, with length at birth recorded at just 0.6 centimeters [Lb = 0.6 centimeters], a value typical of flatfishes with an extended pelagic larval phase. The wet weight at birth is correspondingly slight at 0.0335 grams [Wwb = 0.0335 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves provisioned within eggs that have a diameter ranging from 3.6 to 4.7 millimeters. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are lecithotrophic, undergoing a period of yolk absorption before the onset of exogenous feeding. The ability to capture prey and commence active feeding marks a critical transition, allowing the small larvae to fuel further somatic growth during their drift in ocean currents. Understanding these early-stage metrics provides a foundation for comparing the species with other pleuronectiforms that occupy similar continental slope habitats.

The larval period culminates in a dramatic morphological transformation known as metamorphosis, during which the left eye migrates to the right side of the head as the body plan reorganizes for a benthic existence. This larval-juvenile transition occurs at a total length of approximately 6 centimeters , a threshold that signals the shift from a pelagic, bilaterally symmetrical larva to a demersal, asymmetrical juvenile. Following metamorphic climax and benthic settlement, young individuals adopt a bottom-oriented lifestyle, feeding on crustaceans and small fish in deep waters. The post-metamorphic juvenile stage represents a period of sustained mass gain and progressive somatic development. During these early years on the seafloor, the fish gradually accumulate the body reserves necessary to support future gametogenesis and reproductive activation, a process that unfolds over several seasons in these high-latitude environments where prey availability follows marked seasonal cycles.

Sexual maturation in Greenland halibut is size-dependent rather than strictly age-based, a pattern common among iteroparous deep-sea teleosts. Field studies indicate that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis in females, is attained at a fork length of 62.5 centimeters [Lp = 62.5 centimeters]. This length at puberty is reached after several years of benthic feeding and growth in the cold, food-limited environment of the continental slope. Individuals continue to grow after reaching sexual maturity, with females ultimately attaining a larger asymptotic size than males. The maximum total length recorded for females in the wild reaches 130 centimeters [Li = 130 centimeters], a figure that underscores the pronounced sexual size dimorphism characteristic of this species. This dimorphism likely reflects differential energetic investment strategies, with females allocating substantial resources toward egg production while males invest more heavily in somatic maintenance and foraging activity across their expansive home ranges.

Mature males exhibit a smaller ultimate body size, with the maximum total length reported for this sex reaching 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters]. The difference in asymptotic size between the sexes has direct implications for reproductive output, as larger females can carry more oocytes and produce larger batches of eggs. In terms of mass, the ultimate wet weight for females is substantial at approximately 23,200 grams [Wwi = approximately 23,200 grams], a figure calculated from length-weight regressions based on large specimens. For males, the corresponding ultimate wet weight is lower, reaching about 13,500 grams [Wwi = about 13,500 grams], consistent with their smaller maximum length and less voluminous body shape. These mass values reflect the considerable energetic capital that adult individuals must accumulate and maintain while operating in deep, cold waters where metabolic rates are low but prey resources are patchily distributed across the seabed.

Reproductive output in Greenland halibut is tightly linked to the thermal conditions of their deepwater habitat, particularly the stable temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C] that characterizes much of their depth range. Under these cold conditions, females produce approximately 300,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 300,000 eggs per year], a rate that represents the maximum reproductive output recorded for the species. The maximum lifespan of Greenland halibut has been estimated at 30 years [am = 30 years] when individuals experience the prevailing thermal regime of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], highlighting the slow pace of life in this environment. This remarkable longevity, combined with delayed maturation and moderate fecundity, aligns with expectations for a cold-adapted, deepwater predator. Such a life-history strategy makes the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as recovery from population declines requires many years given the extended generation times inherent in these cold-adapted populations.
